2|name: grpc-expert
3|description: "Expert guidance for gRPC/Protocol Buffers work in the operation-dbus-proto (OP-DBUS) workspace — designing plugin methods, generating .proto/service definitions, wiring the op-grpc-bridge, or fixing plugins with missing gRPC methods. Use this whenever the user mentions gRPC, proto/protobuf, plugin methods, the gRPC bridge, tonic, reflection descriptors, 'missing plugins' in the gRPC diagnostic page, or the seal/freeze/hot pipeline — even if they don't say 'gRPC' explicitly (e.g. 'the plugin isn't showing up on the diagnostic page', 'add a method to plugin X', 'regen protos')."
4|metadata:
5|  version: 1.0.0
6|disable-model-invocation: false
7|---
8|
9|# gRPC Expert — OP-DBUS
10|
11|This workspace does **not** hand-write per-plugin `.proto` files. Proto generation is
12|automatic, driven entirely by each plugin's `PluginSchema`. If you remember one thing
13|from this skill: **fixing a plugin's gRPC surface means editing its Rust schema
14|function, not writing `.proto`.**
15|
16|## The real pipeline (roll → seal → freeze → hot)
17|
18|```
19|1. Plugin declares  → PluginSchema { methods: HashMap<String, MethodDecl>, signals: Vec<SignalDecl>, ... }
20|                       in crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/<plugin>.rs
21|2. Schema gets put   → op-projection's SchemaEngine publishes the catalog hash
22|                       (op_identity::schema_bridge::schema_catalog_hash())
23|3. Sealed by blob    → op-blob seals the plugin object into an immutable blob:
24|                       /dev/shm/opdbus/plugin-blobs/<plugin_id>.<schema_hash16>.blob
25|                       (op-blob is the ONLY writer — never write blobs elsewhere)
26|4. Descriptors       → TWO separate reflection layers exist, don't confuse them:
27|   for reflection       a) STATIC: crates/op-grpc-bridge/build.rs generates
28|                            plugin_methods.proto from every plugin's schema.methods,
29|                            compiles it with tonic_build into operation_descriptor.bin
30|                            (a protobuf FileDescriptorSet), served by tonic-reflection.
31|                         b) DYNAMIC: crates/op-grpc-bridge/src/dynamic_reflection.rs
32|                            (ActiveReflectionCatalog) hydrates live from the sealed
33|                            SHM blob catalog via hydrate_reflection_from_shm() —
34|                            this is the "frozen" descriptor set for what's actually
35|                            present right now, independent of what's compiled in.
36|5. Frozen            → the blob + its descriptors are immutable once sealed.
37|6. gRPC socket = hot → crates/op-grpc-bridge/src/grpc_server.rs registers the
38|                       generated per-plugin service (plugin_method_routes.rs,
39|                       add_routes()) on the tonic UDS bridge, dispatching each
40|                       RPC to call_generated_plugin_method_typed(plugin_id,
41|                       schema_name, ...) which routes through PluginService.CallMethod
42|                       — i.e. gRPC never bypasses D-Bus, it's a bridge, not a
43|                       second control plane.
44|```
45|
46|A plugin shows green/connected on the gRPC diagnostic page **iff**:
47|- its `PluginSchema.methods` is non-empty (empty → `build.rs` silently skips it —
48|  see `collect_plugin_methods()`), **and**
49|- the plugin is sealed in the SHM blob catalog.
50|
51|These are discovery prerequisites, not proof of execution. Canonical dispatch
52|also requires the method's complete declaration and plugin version to match the
53|compiled handler, argument validation, verified identity, and its exact grant.
54|An advertised method whose adapter is absent is unfinished work.
55|
56|## Where to actually make changes
57|
58|| Task | File |
59||---|---|
60|| Add/fix methods for plugin `<name>` | `crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/<name>.rs`, inside `<name>_schema()` |
61|| Reusable input/output builders | `crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/plugin_scaffold_helpers.rs` |
62|| Regenerate the derived `.proto` + routes | Just rebuild — `build.rs` regenerates on every `cargo build -p op-grpc-bridge` (it `rerun-if-changed`s `../op-plugins/src/state_plugins`) |
63|| Wire a genuinely new (non-plugin-derived) service | `crates/op-grpc-bridge/proto/*.proto`, add to the `compile_protos` list + `rerun-if-changed` in `crates/op-grpc-bridge/build.rs`, then register in `crates/op-grpc-bridge/src/grpc_server.rs` |
64|| Inspect what's currently generated | `target/{debug,release}/build/op-grpc-bridge-*/out/plugin_methods.proto` (build artifact — never hand-edit) |
65|
66|**Never** create files under a `/proto/plugin_methods/` directory or a
67|`plugin_methods_unified.proto` by hand — those paths don't exist in this repo and
68|aren't part of the real pipeline; that was a stale spec from an earlier session.
69|The single source of truth is `schema.methods`.
70|
71|## Adding methods to a plugin (the actual workflow)
72|
73|Look at `crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/proxy_server.rs` (`proxy_server_schema()`)
74|for the canonical pattern:
75|
76|```rust
77|use op_state_store::{MethodDecl, PluginSchema, SideEffect};
78|
79|schema.methods.insert(
80|    "start_proxy".to_string(),
81|    method_decl_from_schemars_with_output::<StartProxyInput, plugin_scaffold_helpers::AckOutput>(
82|        "start_proxy",
83|        SideEffect::Mutation,       // Read | Mutation
84|        false,                       // idempotent?
85|        "cap.network.proxy.start@v1",   // required_capability
86|        "mut.network.proxy.start@v1",   // subid — must follow the taxonomy in CLAUDE.md
87|    ),
88|);
89|```
90|
91|- Define `StartProxyInput` (and a typed output struct, or reuse `AckOutput`) as
92|  `#[derive(schemars::JsonSchema)]` structs — the JSON Schema is derived, never
93|  hand-written as `serde_json::json!({...})` unless there's no existing helper.
94|- `method_decl_from_schemars_with_output::<Input, Output>` is the current
95|  (non-deprecated) helper; the single-generic `method_decl_from_schemars` is
96|  deprecated but still present for legacy callers.
97|- `subid` must be registered in the canonical registry per CLAUDE.md
98|  (`crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/oscal_subid_registry.rs`) — CI enforces
99|  uniqueness.
100|- For plugins with **zero** declared methods today (the ones missing from the
101|  diagnostic page), don't hand-author their methods one by one — see
102|  **The Auto-Creator Plugin** below. That's the actual deliverable: a plugin
103|  that finds these gaps and fills them itself, using real research per plugin.
104|
105|## The Auto-Creator Plugin (an ongoing capability, not a one-off batch)
106|
107|This is **not** a one-time task to fix ~11 named plugins. It's a standing
108|system capability: whenever the system encounters *any* missing plugin —
109|now, or a new one added in the future — it automatically generates that
110|plugin and submits it for **human review**, never auto-merges/auto-seals it
111|unreviewed. The current ~11 gaps are just the first real instances that
112|exercise this, not the scope.
113|
114|Consistent with this workspace's "reactive, not polled" principle (CLAUDE.md):
115|this should be triggered by an actual arrival/lookup that reveals the gap
116|(e.g. a D-Bus/gRPC call or reflection lookup against a plugin whose
117|`schema.methods` is empty, or a plugin name that doesn't resolve at all),
118|not a cron-style sweep re-scanning all plugins on a timer.
119|
120|Build it as a plugin itself (same `PluginSchema`/`MethodDecl` pattern as every
121|plugin in `crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/`), whose job is to:
122|
123|1. **Detect a gap on encounter** — when something references a plugin that's
124|   missing or has `schema.methods.is_empty()` (same emptiness check
125|   `build.rs::collect_plugin_methods` already uses to skip plugins), that's
126|   the trigger — not a periodic scan of the whole registry.
127|2. **Research that specific gap** — drive deep research via the **NotebookLM
128|   MCP** (once wired up) to determine what capabilities/operations the
129|   missing plugin should realistically expose, given its existing state
130|   struct (if any), documentation, and prior art from comparable plugins
131|   already in the registry. This replaces guessing or generic Get/List/Watch
132|   stubs with a grounded, plugin-specific proposal.
133|3. **Synthesize typed schemas** — turn the research output into real Rust
134|   input/output structs (`#[derive(schemars::JsonSchema)]`) and `MethodDecl`
135|   entries — per the "no `AckOutput`" rule above, every synthesized method
136|   needs its own meaningful typed request/response, not a generic ack.
137|4. **Submit for human review — do not auto-apply.** The output is a proposed
138|   plugin/schema (e.g. a diff/PR against `<name>_schema()`, or a new
139|   `crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/<name>.rs` for a wholly new plugin),
140|   held for a human to approve before it's merged. Only after human approval
141|   does it enter the normal pipeline (build → proto → reflection → sealed
142|   blob → hot). The auto-creator must never seal a blob or register a plugin
143|   into the live catalog on its own. It never emits `.proto` directly and
144|   never writes to `/proto/plugin_methods/` — the single source of truth
145|   stays `schema.methods`, authored by a human-approved change.
146|
147|In short: this is a **standing, reactive meta-plugin that drafts schemas for
148|whatever plugin is found missing, research-backed via NotebookLM, gated by
149|human review** — not a fixed batch job for a specific list of plugins.
150|
151|## JSON Schema → proto mapping
152|
153|The shared mapper lives in `crates/op-blob/src/json_schema_proto.rs`; the bridge
154|uses it for generated native messages. Structured objects become typed nested
155|messages; typed string-key maps retain their value types. Scalars preserve
156|presence, including explicit false, zero and empty strings. Unsigned 64-bit
157|contracts use `uint64`. Nulls, arbitrary JSON, unions and nested arrays use the
158|appropriate standard `Value`/`Struct`/`ListValue` dependencies. Arbitrary numbers
159|inside `Value` remain subject to protobuf's double-precision limit.
160|
161|Two existing wire layouts have distinct numbering rules: generated native
162|bridge fields use stable FNV-1a numbers; sealed per-method messages retain their
163|sorted sequential numbering. Preserve both layouts. Canonical schema map keys
164|and declared transport method names are separate identities, not interchangeable
165|aliases. Consumers register the original sealed descriptors and never reseal,
166|regenerate, or hash them as an existence check.
167|
168|## Known project-specific tensions vs. generic gRPC best practice
169|
170|Be aware of these before applying textbook advice unmodified:
171|
172|- **Do not use `AckOutput { success: bool }` for new/generated methods.**
173|  It exists in the codebase (see `proxy_server.rs`) as a legacy shortcut for
174|  "no meaningful return value," but every method a plugin exposes should have
175|  a real, dedicated typed **input** struct and typed **output** struct that
176|  reflect what the operation actually consumes and returns — not a generic
177|  bool. This matters especially for the auto-creator (below): when it
178|  synthesizes methods for a previously-empty plugin, it must generate a
179|  specific `<Method>Input` and `<Method>Output` schemars struct per method,
180|  never fall back to `AckOutput`. Errors still go through `tonic::Status` /
181|  D-Bus error replies, never a `success: false` field.
182|- **Enums are flattened to `string`, not real proto `enum`.** JSON Schema
183|  `enum` currently maps to proto `string` (see table above), so the classic
184|  `FOO_STATUS_UNSPECIFIED = 0` convention isn't applied by the generator today.
185|  If asked to add real proto enums, that requires changing
186|  `json_schema_type_to_proto` in `crates/op-grpc-bridge/build.rs`, not just the
187|  plugin schema.
188|- **Streaming comes from state in SHM.** The owner reaffirmed this on
189|  2026-09-13. Methods update authoritative SHM state before notifications;
190|  existing state subscriptions read that state. Current generated method RPCs
191|  being unary does not require another streaming method/service. Preserve
192|  private principal/session scope. Method arguments, event payloads and
193|  generator buffers are not independent state authorities, and buffered unary
194|  responses are not a substitute for SHM state streaming.
195|- **One generated file per bridge crate**, not the "1-1-1" file-per-message
196|  convention — `plugin_methods.proto` bundles every plugin's messages/services
197|  in one generated file. That's fine; it's a build artifact, not hand-maintained
198|  source, so the usual "small modular .proto files" guidance doesn't apply to it.
199|
200|## Generic protobuf/gRPC conventions (still apply to hand-written `.proto`)
201|
202|For any `.proto` you *do* hand-write (domain services under
203|`crates/op-grpc-bridge/proto/`, not plugin-derived ones):
204|
205|- `snake_case` field names, `CamelCase` message/service/RPC names, package names
206|  lowercase (this repo uses `operation.plugin.v1`-style packages).
207|- Reserve field numbers for removed fields; never reuse them.
208|- Prefer `optional` for fields that may be absent; avoid letting one field's
209|  value change the semantic meaning of another.
210|- Real proto `enum`s (where you control the generator, e.g. hand-written
211|  services) always start with `..._UNSPECIFIED = 0`.
212|- Use gRPC status codes (`tonic::Status`) for error paths; reserve response
213|  message fields for actual data.
214|- TLS is mandatory in this workspace (per CLAUDE.md zero-trust transport) —
215|  never wire a new gRPC service as plaintext, even over UDS.
216|- Server reflection (`tonic-reflection`) must stay wired for every new service
217|  so it's discoverable by `op-cognitive-mcp` and the gRPC diagnostic page —
218|  don't add a service that bypasses reflection registration.
219|
220|## Quick diagnostic checklist
221|
222|If a plugin isn't showing up / isn't callable over gRPC:
223|
224|1. Does `crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/<name>.rs`'s `<name>_schema()`
225|   actually populate `schema.methods`? (Empty → `build.rs` skips it entirely.)
226|2. Is the plugin registered via `inventory::submit! { PluginReg::new(...) }` in
227|   its own file (self-registration — check `crates/op-plugins/src/default_registry.rs`
228|   only if the plugin doesn't show up in `available_plugins()` at all)?
229|3. Did `cargo build -p op-grpc-bridge` actually rerun? (`build.rs` only reruns on
230|   changes under `../op-plugins/src/state_plugins` or `build.rs` itself.)
231|4. Is the plugin actually **sealed** in the SHM blob catalog
232|   (`/dev/shm/opdbus/plugin-blobs/`)? Static compiled-in proto support and the
233|   *dynamic* "hot" reflection/routing are two different gates — a plugin can
234|   compile fine and still be invisible if it was never sealed.","total_lines":234,"file_size":14428,"truncated":false,"is_binary":false,"is_image":false,"not_found":false}

2|name: ovs-db-analysis
3|description: >-
4|  Analyze Open vSwitch data from sosreport — conf.db, OpenFlow dumps, port stats,
5|  tunnels, and datapath health. Use when troubleshooting OVS packet drops, flow
6|  performance, bridge/port/interface issues, DPDK vs kernel datapath, or when the
7|  user mentions sosreport openvswitch, ovs-ofctl, ovsdb-tool, or ovs-db-analysis.
8|---
9|
10|# OVS Database and Flow Analysis
11|
12|This skill provides detailed analysis of Open vSwitch (OVS) data collected via sosreport. It operates in four modes:
13|
14|1. **Default mode**: Full analysis - conf.db + all text files (requires ovsdb-tool, falls back to text files if not available)
15|2. **Database mode (`--db`)**: Database only - analyze conf.db (requires ovsdb-tool)
16|3. **Text files mode (`--flows-only`)**: Text files only - no ovsdb-tool needed
17|4. **Query mode (`--query`)**: Run custom OVSDB JSON queries (requires ovsdb-tool)
18|
19|## When to Use This Skill
20|
21|Use this skill when:
22|- **Troubleshooting packet drops** - Find drop flows being hit
23|- **Analyzing flow performance** - View top flows by packet count
24|- Analyzing OVS configuration from a sosreport
25|- Troubleshooting bridge, port, or interface issues
26|- Investigating DPDK vs kernelspace datapath
27|- Reviewing tunnel configurations (VXLAN, Geneve, GRE)
28|- Checking port statistics (drops, errors, traffic)
29|- Mapping Kubernetes pods to OVS interfaces
30|
31|## Prerequisites
32|
33|**Default mode** (full analysis):
34|- **ovsdb-tool** must be installed (from openvswitch package)
35|- Falls back to `--flows-only` if ovsdb-tool not found
36|- Sosreport with `sos_commands/openvswitch/` directory and `conf.db`
37|
38|**Database mode** (`--db`):
39|- **ovsdb-tool** must be installed (from openvswitch package)
40|  - Check: `which ovsdb-tool`
41|  - Fedora/RHEL: `sudo dnf install openvswitch`
42|  - Ubuntu/Debian: `sudo apt install openvswitch-common`
43|- Sosreport with `conf.db` file
44|
45|**Text files mode** (`--flows-only`):
46|- No special tools needed - works out of the box!
47|- Sosreport with `sos_commands/openvswitch/` directory
48|
49|**Query mode** (`--query`):
50|- **ovsdb-tool** must be installed
51|- Incompatible with `--flows-only`
52|
53|## File Locations in Sosreport
54|
55|The sosreport collects:
56|```
57|sosreport-hostname-date/
58|├── etc/openvswitch/conf.db              (OVS database - for --db mode)
59|├── var/lib/openvswitch/conf.db          (alternate location)
60|└── sos_commands/openvswitch/            (default mode uses these)
61|    ├── ovs-vsctl_-t_5_show              (topology)
62|    ├── ovs-vsctl_-t_5_list_bridge       (bridge details)
63|    ├── ovs-vsctl_-t_5_list_interface    (interface details)
64|    ├── ovs-vsctl_-t_5_list_Open_vSwitch (system info)
65|    ├── ovs-ofctl_dump-flows_<bridge>    (OpenFlow entries)
66|    ├── ovs-ofctl_dump-ports_<bridge>    (Port statistics)
67|    ├── ovs-appctl_coverage.show         (internal stats)
68|    ├── ovs-appctl_upcall.show           (datapath health)
69|    ├── ovs-appctl_tnl.ports.show_-v     (tunnel ports)
70|    └── ...
71|```
72|
73|## Analysis Script
74|
75|The analysis script is located at:
76|```
77|<plugin-root>/skills/ovs-db-analysis/scripts/analyze_ovs_db.py
78|```
79|
80|## Implementation Steps
81|
82|### Step 1: Locate the Analysis Script
83|
84|```bash
85|SCRIPT_PATH=$(find ~ -name "analyze_ovs_db.py" -path "*/sosreport/skills/ovs-db-analysis/scripts/*" 2>/dev/null | head -1)
86|
87|if [ -z "$SCRIPT_PATH" ]; then
88|    echo "ERROR: analyze_ovs_db.py script not found."
89|    exit 1
90|fi
91|```
92|
93|### Step 2: Run the Analysis
94|
95|```bash
96|# Default: Full analysis - conf.db + text files (requires ovsdb-tool)
97|python3 "$SCRIPT_PATH" /path/to/sosreport-hostname-date/
98|
99|# Analyze from archive
100|python3 "$SCRIPT_PATH" /path/to/sosreport-hostname-date.tar.xz
101|
102|# Database only mode (requires ovsdb-tool)
103|python3 "$SCRIPT_PATH" /path/to/sosreport/ --db
104|
105|# Text files only mode (no ovsdb-tool needed)
106|python3 "$SCRIPT_PATH" /path/to/sosreport/ --flows-only
107|```
108|
109|### Step 3: Custom Queries (Optional, requires --db)
110|
111|For specific investigations, use raw OVSDB queries:
112|
113|```bash
114|# Query all bridges
115|python3 "$SCRIPT_PATH" /path/to/sosreport/ --query '["Open_vSwitch", {"op":"select", "table":"Bridge", "where":[], "columns":["name","datapath_type","fail_mode"]}]'
116|
117|# Query VXLAN interfaces
118|python3 "$SCRIPT_PATH" /path/to/sosreport/ --query '["Open_vSwitch", {"op":"select", "table":"Interface", "where":[["type","==","vxlan"]], "columns":["name","options"]}]'
119|
120|# Query interfaces with errors
121|python3 "$SCRIPT_PATH" /path/to/sosreport/ --query '["Open_vSwitch", {"op":"select", "table":"Interface", "where":[], "columns":["name","error"]}]'
122|```
123|
124|## Analysis Output
125|
126|The default mode analyzes:
127|
128|| Analysis | Source File | Description |
129||----------|-------------|-------------|
130|| System Info | `ovs-vsctl_-t_5_list_Open_vSwitch` | OVS/DPDK version, system type, external IDs |
131|| Topology | `ovs-vsctl_-t_5_show` | Bridge overview with ports grouped by type |
132|| Bridge Details | `ovs-vsctl_-t_5_list_bridge` | Datapath type, fail mode, CT zones |
133|| Interfaces | `ovs-vsctl_-t_5_list_interface` | By type, pod interfaces with mapping |
134|| OpenFlow | `ovs-ofctl_dump-flows_*` | Flow counts, drops, top flows |
135|| Port Stats | `ovs-ofctl_dump-ports_*` | RX/TX drops and errors |
136|| Tunnels | `ovs-appctl_tnl.ports.show_-v` | Configured tunnel ports |
137|| Datapath Health | `ovs-appctl_upcall.show` | Flow table usage vs limit |
138|| OVS Stats | `ovs-appctl_coverage.show` | Internal counters (netlink, OVSDB, etc.) |
139|
140|## OpenFlow Analysis Features
141|
142|| Feature | Description |
143||---------|-------------|
144|| Flow Count | Total flows per bridge (total, drop, with hits) |
145|| Drop Detection | Flows with `actions=drop` that have packet hits |
146|| Top Flows | Most active flows sorted by n_packets |
147|| Table Distribution | Flow counts per OpenFlow table |
148|| Port Drops | RX/TX drop counters per port |
149|| Port Errors | RX/TX error counters per port |
150|| Datapath Health | Flow table usage vs limit (from upcall.show) |
151|| OVS Stats | Internal statistics (netlink, OpenFlow, OVSDB transactions) |
152|
153|## OVN Internal Tables (Ignore Drops in These)
154|
155|When analyzing drop flows in OVN-managed bridges (br-int), **ignore drops in table 44 and tables 64-87** as these are internal OVN mechanics, not security policy or real packet drops.
156|
157|> **⚠️ Note:** OVN and OVS are complex systems and table mappings can change between releases. Always verify drop analysis against the specific OVN version in use. When in doubt, check the OVN source code for your release.
158|
159|| Table | Name | Purpose |
160||-------|------|---------|
161|| **44** | **CHK_LB_OUTPUT** | **Loopback prevention - drops packets that would loop back (high volume, normal)** |
162|| 64 | SAVE_INPORT | Save ingress port for later |
163|| 65 | LOG_TO_PHY | Logical to physical mapping |
164|| 66 | MAC_BINDING | MAC binding lookups |
165|| 67 | MAC_LOOKUP | MAC address table lookups |
166|| 68-69 | CHK_LB_HAIRPIN | Load balancer hairpin checks |
167|| 70 | CT_SNAT_HAIRPIN | Conntrack SNAT hairpin |
168|| 71-72 | GET/LOOKUP_FDB | FDB (forwarding DB) lookups |
169|| 73-74 | CHK_IN_PORT_SEC | Ingress port security |
170|| 75 | CHK_OUT_PORT_SEC | Egress port security |
171|| 76-77 | ECMP_NH | ECMP next-hop handling |
172|| 78 | CHK_LB_AFFINITY | Load balancer affinity |
173|| **79** | **MAC_CACHE_USE** | **MAC cache miss (high volume, normal)** |
174|| 80 | CT_ZONE_LOOKUP | Conntrack zone lookup |
175|| 81-83 | CT_ORIG_*_LOAD | Conntrack original tuple loading |
176|| 84 | FLOOD_REMOTE_CHASSIS | Remote chassis flooding |
177|| 85 | CT_STATE_SAVE | Conntrack state save |
178|| 86 | CT_ORIG_PROTO_LOAD | Conntrack protocol loading |
179|| 87 | GET_REMOTE_FDB | Remote FDB lookup |
180|
181|**Relevant drop tables for troubleshooting:**
182|- **Table 9**: Ingress ACLs - actual policy drops (look for `reg0=0x8000`)
183|- **Table 0**: Initial classification drops
184|- **Tables < 64**: Generally meaningful drops
185|
186|## Common Analysis Scenarios
187|
188|### 1. Troubleshooting Packet Drops
189|
190|```bash
191|# Quick analysis (default mode, no ovsdb-tool)
192|python3 "$SCRIPT_PATH" /path/to/sosreport/
193|```
194|
195|Look for:
196|- **ACTIVE DROP FLOWS** section showing flows dropping packets
197|- **PORT STATISTICS** showing ports with drops/errors
198|
199|### 2. Checking DPDK Configuration
200|
201|```bash
202|# Default mode shows DPDK info from text files
203|python3 "$SCRIPT_PATH" /path/to/sosreport/
204|
205|# Or use database mode for custom queries
206|python3 "$SCRIPT_PATH" /path/to/sosreport/ --query '["Open_vSwitch", {"op":"select", "table":"Open_vSwitch", "where":[], "columns":["dpdk_initialized","other_config"]}]'
207|```
208|
209|### 3. Investigating Pod Connectivity
210|
211|The interface analysis shows pod-to-OVS mapping:
212|- Interfaces with `external_ids` containing `iface-id`
213|- Interface names ending with `_h` (veth host side)
214|
215|### 4. Datapath Health Check
216|
217|The upcall stats show:
218|```
219|DATAPATH FLOW TABLE HEALTH
220|  Current flows: 155 / 200,000 (0.1% used)
221|  Average: 156, Max seen: 215
222|  ✓ Flow table healthy
223|```
224|
225|If usage > 90%, flows are being evicted too aggressively.

2|name: kernel-fuse-diagnosis
3|description: >
4|  FUSE（用户态文件系统）内核端故障诊断技能。当用户提到 FUSE 文件系统 hang、
5|  所有操作返回 EIO、FUSE daemon 崩溃/重启、请求队列阻塞、D 状态进程堆积、
6|  /sys/fs/fuse/connections/ 异常、libfuse 兼容性、max_read/max_write 配置不当、
7|  writeback cache 一致性问题、多线程 FUSE daemon 死锁、容器中 /dev/fuse 权限问题、
8|  FUSE 性能退化等关键词时，必须使用本技能。
9|  覆盖场景：FUSE daemon 崩溃后 EIO、请求队列阻塞与 D 状态、max_read/max_write 配置不当、
10|  writeback cache 一致性问题、多线程 daemon 死锁、/dev/fuse 权限问题、内核 FUSE 模块 Bug、
11|  混合复杂 FUSE 故障。即使只收到"文件系统挂了"、"目录打不开"、"ls 卡死"但挂载点
12|  为 FUSE 类型时也应触发本技能。
13|  支持 FUSE 全链路诊断（sysfs 队列 → 内核参数 → daemon 进程 → 代码级根因）。
14|---
15|
16|# FUSE 内核端故障诊断（三层下钻：系统层 → 类型层 → 代码根因层）
17|
18|## 第一节：故障目录结构
19|
20|```text
21|fuse_case/                  # 故障案例目录
22|├── scripts/                # 【内置】本技能的诊断脚本
23|│   ├── 01_baseline_info.sh
24|│   ├── branch_A_daemon_crash.sh
25|│   ├── branch_B_req_queue.sh
26|│   ├── branch_C_max_read_write.sh
27|│   ├── branch_D_writeback_cache.sh
28|│   ├── branch_E_mt_deadlock.sh
29|│   ├── branch_F_dev_fuse_perm.sh
30|│   ├── branch_G_kernel_bug.sh
31|│   └── branch_H_mixed.sh
32|├── logs/                   # 【可选】应用日志
33|│   ├── application.log
34|│   └── dmesg_output.txt
35|├── fuse_state/             # 【可选】故障时刻的 FUSE 状态快照
36|│   ├── connections.txt     # ls /sys/fs/fuse/connections/
37|│   ├── waiting.txt         # cat .../waiting
38|│   └── abort.txt           # cat .../abort
39|└── report/                 # 【输出】诊断报告目录
40|```
41|
42|```bash
43|# 检查 FUSE 文件系统挂载状态基线
44|mount -t fuse
45|```

48|
49|## 第二节：分析策略（三层下钻，逐层收敛）
50|
51|FUSE 内核端故障诊断采用**三层下钻模型**，从最外层逐层深入，层间存在依赖关系：
52|
53|```
54|┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
55|│                   三层下钻分析模型                                 │
56|│                                                                 │
57|│   L1: 系统层         mount -t fuse /proc/mounts                 │
58|│       │               /sys/fs/fuse/connections/*                │
59|│       └─ 判断：FUSE 挂载点是否正常？连接是否存在？               │
60|│                                                                 │
61|│   L2: 类型层         strace -p <daemon_pid>                     │
62|│       │               cat /sys/fs/fuse/connections/*/waiting     │
63|│       └─ 判断：是 EIO？请求阻塞？性能退化？权限问题？            │
64|│                                                                 │
65|│   L3: 代码/内核层    FUSE daemon 源码分析                       │
66|│                      内核 FUSE 模块参数 (/sys/module/fuse/)     │
67|│                      /dev/fuse 设备状态                          │
68|│                      └─ 根因定位：daemon 崩溃 / 队列阻塞 / 配置  │
69|│                                                                 │
70|│   每层输出：证据 + 结论。L3 输出最终根因。                       │
71|└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
72|```
73|
74|### 故障分类树
75|
76|```
77|L1 ─ FUSE 挂载点与连接检查
78|│
79|├─ L2 ─ 挂载点正常？─────── 否 ──→ 非 FUSE 问题，转其他技能
80|│                         是
81|│                         ↓
82|├─ L2 ─ 操作返回 EIO？──── 是 ──→ Branch A (Daemon Crash)
83|│                         否
84|│                         ↓
85|├─ L2 ─ 进程 D 状态/Hang？ 是 ──→ Branch B (Req Queue) / Branch E (MT Deadlock)
86|│                         否
87|│                         ↓
88|├─ L2 ─ 性能退化？─────── 是 ──→ Branch C (Max Read/Write)
89|│                         否
90|│                         ↓
91|├─ L2 ─ 数据一致性异常？─ 是 ──→ Branch D (Writeback Cache)
92|│                         否
93|│                         ↓
94|├─ L2 ─ 权限问题？─────── 是 ──→ Branch F (dev/fuse Perm)
95|│                         否
96|│                         ↓
97|├─ L2 ─ 内核崩溃/Oops？── 是 ──→ Branch G (Kernel Bug)
98|│                         否
99|│                         ↓
100|└─ L2 ─ 混合/复杂现象？── 是 ──→ Branch H (Mixed)
101|```

104|
105|## 第三节：诊断流程
106|
107|### L1: 系统层 — 基线采集与挂载点检查
108|
109|检查系统 FUSE 基础配置与挂载状态，判断是否为系统级配置问题。
110|
111|```bash
112|# 1. 检查 FUSE 挂载点
113|mount -t fuse
114|
115|# 2. 检查 /proc/mounts 中 FUSE 条目
116|grep fuse /proc/mounts
117|
118|# 3. 检查 FUSE 内核连接状态
119|ls /sys/fs/fuse/connections/ 2>/dev/null
120|
121|# 4. 检查 FUSE daemon 进程
122|ps aux | grep -E "[f]use|[F]ILESYSTEM_NAME"
123|
124|# 5. 基本连通性测试
125|ls -la <FUSE_mount_point>
126|stat <FUSE_mount_point>/test_file 2>&1
127|```
128|
129|**L1 结论判定**：
130|
131|| 现象 | 可能原因 | 下一层 |
132||------|---------|--------|
133|| 挂载点 ls 返回 EIO | FUSE daemon 崩溃 | Branch A |
134|| ls 卡死/D 状态 | 请求队列阻塞 | Branch B |
135|| 性能异常慢 | max_read/max_write 配置不当 | Branch C |
136|| 数据不一致 | writeback cache 问题 | Branch D |
137|| daemon 进程存在但无响应 | 多线程死锁 | Branch E |
138|| 权限 denied | /dev/fuse 权限 | Branch F |
139|| 内核 Panic/Oops | FUSE 内核模块 Bug | Branch G |
140|| 多种现象共存 | 混合故障 | Branch H |
141|
142|### L2 → L3: 类型层与代码根因层
143|
144|#### Branch A — FUSE Daemon 崩溃后 EIO
145|
146|**触发条件**：L1 中访问 FUSE 挂载点返回 "Transport endpoint is not connected" 或 EIO。
147|
148|```
149|L2 诊断：
150|├── 1. stat <mount_point>（确认 EIO 错误码）
151|├── 2. grep <mount_point> /proc/mounts（挂载条目是否仍存在）
152|├── 3. ls /sys/fs/fuse/connections/（连接是否已销毁）
153|├── 4. ps aux | grep <daemon_name>（daemon 进程是否存在）
154|├── 5. journalctl -u <daemon_service> --since "5 min ago"（daemon 退出日志）
155|├── 6. dmesg | grep -i fuse（内核 FUSE 消息）
156|├── 7. cat /sys/fs/fuse/connections/*/abort 2>/dev/null（abort 状态）
157|│
158|└── L3 根因判定：
159|    ├── daemon 进程不存在 + 连接已销毁 → daemon 崩溃/被 OOM Kill
160|    ├── daemon 进程不存在 + 连接残留 → daemon 退出但连接未清理
161|    ├── daemon 存在但连接状态异常 → daemon 内部状态机错误
162|    ├── dmesg 显示 "fuse: aborting connection" → 内核主动中止
163|    ├── OOM Killer 日志 → daemon 因内存超限被内核杀死
164|    └── 连接 abort 状态为 1 → 手动触发 abort 或 daemon 调用 abort
165|```
166|
167|**典型输出**：
168|```
169|结论: FUSE daemon 进程不存在（已崩溃），
170|      /sys/fs/fuse/connections/ 目录为空（连接已销毁）。
171|      dmesg 无 FUSE 相关错误，但 journalctl 显示 daemon 因
172|      SIGSEGV (signal 11) 退出。
173|根因: FUSE daemon 程序存在内存访问越界 Bug，导致段错误崩溃。
174|```
175|
176|#### Branch B — FUSE 请求队列阻塞
177|
178|**触发条件**：LS 卡死、进程 D 状态（uninterruptible sleep）、`/sys/fs/fuse/connections/*/waiting` 持续增长。
179|
180|```
181|L2 诊断：
182|├── 1. cat /sys/fs/fuse/connections/*/waiting（请求队列深度）
183|├── 2. cat /sys/fs/fuse/connections/*/max_background（最大后台请求数）
184|├── 3. ps aux | grep D | grep -v grep（D 状态进程列表）
185|├── 4. cat /proc/<D_pid>/stack（查看 D 状态内核栈）
186|├── 5. strace -e trace=write,read,ioctl -p <daemon_pid>（daemon 系统调用）
187|├── 6. cat /sys/fs/fuse/connections/*/congested_threshold_ms（拥塞阈值）
188|├── 7. dmesg | grep -i "fuse.*block"（阻塞告警）
189|│
190|└── L3 根因判定：
191|    ├── waiting 持续增长 + daemon 未处理请求 → daemon 侧线程阻塞
192|    ├── daemon 进程 strace 显示 read() 未被唤醒 → 内核/FUSE 调度问题
193|    ├── D 状态进程内核栈显示 fuse_request_send → 请求队列已满等待
194|    ├── max_background 设置过小 → 请求队列排队上限低导致积压
195|    ├── daemon write() 变慢或阻塞 → daemon 后端存储 I/O 瓶颈
196|    └── congested_threshold 触发 → FUSE 内核主动限流
197|```
198|
199|**典型输出**：
200|```
201|结论: /sys/fs/fuse/connections/*/waiting 持续增长（当前值: 512），
202|      进程 D 状态栈显示 fuse_request_send。
203|      strace 显示 daemon read() 调用未被及时唤醒。
204|根因: FUSE daemon 工作线程池太小或线程卡在后端 I/O 上，
205|      无法及时消费内核下发的 FUSE 请求。
206|```
207|
208|#### Branch C — max_read/max_write 配置不当
209|
210|**触发条件**：FUSE 文件系统性能显著低于预期，小文件/大文件读写性能异常。
211|
212|```
213|L2 诊断：
214|├── 1. cat /sys/fs/fuse/connections/*/max_read（当前 FUSE 最大读取大小）
215|├── 2. cat /sys/module/fuse/parameters/max_read（内核模块参数）
216|├── 3. mount | grep <fuse_type>（挂载参数 -o max_read=,max_write=）
217|├── 4. dd if=<mount_point>/test of=/dev/null bs=1M count=100（读性能测试）
218|├── 5. dd if=/dev/zero of=<mount_point>/test bs=1M count=100（写性能测试）
219|├── 6. iostat -x 1 <device>（底层 I/O 延迟）
220|├── 7. strace -e pread64,pwrite64 -p <daemon_pid>（系统调用大小对比）
221|│
222|└── L3 根因判定：
223|    ├── max_read=4096（4K）→ 每次读请求仅传输 4K，大文件读性能极差
224|    ├── max_write=4096（4K）→ 每次写请求仅传输 4K，写性能瓶颈
225|    ├── max_read 与底层存储块大小不匹配 → 产生大量小 I/O
226|    ├── 挂载时未指定 max_read= → 使用默认值（通常 1MB，但某些 FUSE 缩减）
227|    ├── daemon 未实现 readdir 缓存 → 目录遍历性能退化
228|    └── 内核 max_read 参数被 sysfs 限制 → 无法超过内核模块设置的上限
229|```
230|
231|**典型输出**：
232|```
233|结论: max_read=4096（4K），远低于默认 1MB。
234|      dd 读测试仅 12 MB/s，远低于预期 200+ MB/s。
235|      strace 确认每次 pread64 仅传输 4096 字节。
236|根因: FUSE 挂载时未指定 max_read，daemon 初始化协商值为 4K
237|      （libfuse 旧版本默认），导致大文件顺序读性能退化。
238|```
239|
240|#### Branch D — Writeback Cache 一致性问题
241|
242|**触发条件**：FUSE 文件系统写入后读取数据不一致、写入顺序错误、重复内容。
243|
244|```
245|L2 诊断：
246|├── 1. mount | grep <fuse_type> | grep -o "writeback_cache"（检查是否启用）
247|├── 2. cat /sys/module/fuse/parameters/use_writeback_cache（内核参数）
248|├── 3. echo "test" > <mount_point>/file && cat <mount_point>/file（一致性测试）
249|├── 4. strace -e write,pwrite64,fsync -p <daemon_pid>（跟踪写操作时序）
250|├── 5. dd if=/dev/urandom of=<mount_point>/test bs=4K count=100（并发写入）
251|├── 6. md5sum <mount_point>/test && sleep 1 && md5sum <mount_point>/test（变化检测）
252|├── 7. grep -i "fuse.*invalidate" /proc/<daemon_pid>/stack（缓存无效化状态）
253|│
254|└── L3 根因判定：
255|    ├── writeback_cache 启用但 daemon 未实现 ->release 回调 → 数据未刷入后端
256|    ├── 并发写入后的读取返回过期数据 → page cache 未正确无效化
257|    ├── daemon write() 返回成功但数据未持久化 → 缺少 fsync 语义
258|    ├── 内核 fuse_conn 中 writeback_cache=1 但后端不支持原子写
259|    ├── mmap 写入后数据丢失 → FUSE 不支持 shared mmap writeback cache
260|    └── multi-page writeback 顺序错误 → daemon 未按 LBA 顺序处理请求
261|```
262|
263|**典型输出**：
264|```
265|结论: writeback_cache 启用后，写入 100 个 4K 块后的 md5sum
266|      在不同读取时间点返回不同值。
267|      daemon 未实现 ->write() 回调的完整 writeback 语义。
268|根因: FUSE daemon 启用 writeback_cache 模式但未正确处理
269|      内核的 writeback 请求，page cache 与后端存储数据不一致。
270|```
271|
272|#### Branch E — 多线程 FUSE Daemon 死锁
273|
274|**触发条件**：FUSE daemon 进程存在但操作挂起，挂载点操作无响应。
275|
276|```
277|L2 诊断：
278|├── 1. ps -eLf | grep <daemon_name>（daemon 线程列表）
279|├── 2. cat /proc/<daemon_pid>/stack（主线程内核栈）
280|├── 3. for tid in $(ls /proc/<daemon_pid>/task/); do echo "TID:$tid"; cat /proc/$tid/stack 2>/dev/null; done
281|├── 4. strace -f -e trace=write,read,ioctl -p <daemon_pid>（多线程追踪）
282|├── 5. gdb -p <daemon_pid> -batch -ex "thread apply all bt"（全线程回溯）
283|├── 6. cat /sys/fs/fuse/connections/*/waiting（确认请求堆积）
284|├── 7. kill -USR1 <daemon_pid>（向 daemon 发送信号检查状态）
285|│
286|└── L3 根因判定：
287|    ├── 所有工作线程在 pthread_mutex_lock 等待 → 互斥锁死锁
288|    ├── 线程 A 持有锁 L1 等待锁 L2，线程 B 持有锁 L2 等待锁 L1 → 经典死锁
289|    ├── 工作线程在 write() 后端存储时阻塞 → I/O 死锁（等待自身填充）
290|    ├── 线程池所有线程都在 fuse_session_process 中 → 请求循环依赖
291|    ├── 主线程在 fuse_loop 中阻塞但工作线程已退出 → 线程管理 Bug
292|    └── daemon 中 fuse_reply_* 调用顺序错误 → 协议级死锁
293|```
294|
295|**典型输出**：
296|```
297|结论: daemon 4 个工作线程全部在 pthread_mutex_lock 等待。
298|      gdb 显示 Thread 1 持有 lock A 等待 lock B，
299|      Thread 2 持有 lock B 等待 lock A——经典 ABBA 死锁。
300|根因: FUSE daemon 中锁获取顺序不一致，导致多线程死锁，
301|      文件系统操作完全挂起。
302|```
303|
304|#### Branch F — /dev/fuse 设备权限问题
305|
306|**触发条件**：容器或非 root 用户启动 FUSE daemon 时出现 Permission denied。
307|
308|```
309|L2 诊断：
310|├── 1. ls -la /dev/fuse（设备节点权限）
311|├── 2. getfacl /dev/fuse（ACL 权限检查）
312|├── 3. cat /proc/<daemon_pid>/status | grep Cap（daemon 能力集）
313|├── 4. grep fuse /etc/group（fuse 用户组）
314|├── 5. groups <daemon_user>（用户所属组）
315|├── 6. cat /etc/fuse.conf（FUSE 全局配置）
316|├── 7. capsh --print | grep fuse（进程能力检查）
317|├── 8. container environment: cat /proc/1/cgroup（容器内 cgroup 检查）
318|│
319|└── L3 根因判定：
320|    ├── /dev/fuse 权限 0600 root:root → 非 root 用户无法访问
321|    ├── daemon 用户不在 fuse 组 → 缺少 /dev/fuse 访问权限
322|    ├── 容器内未挂载 /dev/fuse → 设备节点不存在
323|    ├── 容器缺少 CAP_SYS_ADMIN 或 CAP_MKNOD → 无法操作 FUSE 设备
324|    ├── user_allow_other 未在 /etc/fuse.conf 启用 → 无法使用 allow_other
325|    ├── AppArmor/SELinux 阻止 FUSE 操作 → 安全策略限制
326|    └── daemon 进程 capabilities 被移除 → container runtime 降权
327|```
328|
329|**典型输出**：
330|```
331|结论: /dev/fuse 权限 0600 root:root，daemon 以非 root 用户
332|      运行且不在 fuse 用户组中。
333|      daemon 启动日志显示 "Permission denied" 打开 /dev/fuse。
334|根因: /dev/fuse 设备节点仅 root 可读写，FUSE daemon
335|      以普通用户运行且未加入 fuse 组，无法打开设备。
336|```
337|
338|#### Branch G — FUSE 内核模块 Bug
339|
340|**触发条件**：内核 Panic、Oops、soft lockup 与 FUSE 相关，或已知 FUSE 内核 Bug。
341|
342|```
343|L2 诊断：
344|├── 1. dmesg | grep -iE "fuse|libfuse"（内核 FUSE 消息）
345|├── 2. dmesg | grep -iE "kernel panic|Oops|BUG|soft lockup"（内核异常）
346|├── 3. cat /sys/module/fuse/version（FUSE 模块版本）
347|├── 4. uname -r（内核版本）
348|├── 5. cat /proc/self/mounts | grep fuse（所有 FUSE 挂载）
349|├── 6. cat /sys/fs/fuse/connections/*/abort（abort 状态）
350|├── 7. test -f /var/crash/vmcore* 2>/dev/null && ls -lh /var/crash/（crash dump 检查）
351|├── 8. grep -i fuse /var/log/messages | tail -20（系统日志）
352|│
353|└── L3 根因判定：
354|    ├── 已知 FUSE 内核 Bug 列表匹配（CVE-xxxx-xxxx / 内核 commit）
355|    ├── 特定内核版本 + FUSE 版本组合已知不兼容
356|    ├── CR2 地址在 FUSE 模块区域内 → FUSE 内核模块导致 Panic
357|    ├── soft lockup 栈显示在 fuse_* 函数中 → FUSE 内核路径问题
358|    ├── 大规模并发操作触发的竞态条件 → 内核 FUSE 并发 Bug
359|    └── FUSE 模块参数不合理导致内核异常 → max_read 过小/过大
360|```
361|
362|**典型输出**：
363|```
364|结论: dmesg 显示 "kernel BUG at fs/fuse/dev.c:1234"，
365|      内核版本 5.15.0-rc3 存在已知 FUSE 并发访问 Bug。
366|      CR2 地址 0xffff888123456789 在 fuse_dev_do_write 函数范围内。
367|根因: 内核 FUSE 模块在特定内核版本下存在并发竞态条件，
368|      多线程并发写操作触发内核 BUG。
369|```
370|
371|#### Branch H — 混合/复杂 FUSE 故障
372|
373|**触发条件**：多种现象共存，或以上分支无法覆盖的复杂 FUSE 问题。
374|
375|```
376|L2 诊断：
377|├── 1. 执行所有以上分支的 L2 诊断（汇总所有证据）
378|├── 2. 交叉对比各分支症状（判定主次故障）
379|├── 3. 完整 strace -f -e trace=all -p <daemon_pid> -o /tmp/strace.log
380|├── 4. lsof -p <daemon_pid>（daemon 打开的文件/连接）
381|├── 5. tcpdump -i any host <backend_storage_ip>（后端存储网络抓包）
382|├── 6. strace -e trace=all ls -la <mount_point> 2>&1（客户端操作全追踪）
383|├── 7. 对比故障前后的 FUSE 配置快照（连接数、参数、daemon 版本）
384|│
385|└── L3 根因判定：
386|    ├── 按故障链优先级排序（先解决依赖的下层问题）
387|    ├── 多故障串联（daemon 崩溃 → 残留连接 → 新 daemon 无法挂载）
388|    ├── 配置错误叠加（max_read 过小 + 线程池太小 + writeback 未启用）
389|    ├── 环境变化触发（内核升级、cgroup 限制、SELinux 策略变更）
390|    └── 复杂的 libfuse API 使用错误（回调注册、会话管理、信号处理）
391|```
392|
393|**典型输出**：
394|```
395|结论: 多种故障共存：daemon 线程池过小（4 线程）导致写性能差，
396|      同时 max_read=4K 进一步退化读性能，writeback cache 启用
397|      但 daemon 未正确处理 ->write 回调。
398|根因: 多重配置叠加导致 FUSE 极端性能退化，建议逐一修复：
399|      1. 增大线程池至 16+
400|      2. 设置 max_read=128K+
401|      3. 检查 writeback cache 回调实现
402|```

3|description: Build, debug, and review Linux FUSE filesystems with the official libfuse userspace library. Use when implementing a FUSE filesystem, choosing between libfuse high-level vs low-level APIs, wiring callbacks, building with fuse3/pkg-config, mounting for local testing, or troubleshooting fusermount3 and permission issues.
4|---
5|
6|# FUSE
7|
8|Use the official `libfuse/libfuse` project as the baseline for Linux FUSE work.
9|
10|## Quick Start
11|
12|1. Confirm the task is Linux FUSE userspace work, not kernel module work.
13|2. Prefer the official `libfuse` interfaces and examples before suggesting wrappers.
14|3. Decide API style:
15|- Use the high-level API for simpler path-based filesystems.
16|- Use the low-level API for inode-level control, explicit replies, or advanced behavior.
17|4. Build with `pkg-config fuse3 --cflags --libs` unless the project already uses another build system.
18|5. For local runs, prefer foreground debug mode first: `-f -d`.
19|
20|## Workflow
21|
22|### 1. Choose the API
23|
24|Use the high-level API when the user needs a straightforward filesystem and path callbacks are sufficient.
25|Read `include/fuse.h` semantics first.
26|
27|Use the low-level API when the user needs inode handling, async-style explicit replies, or finer control over request lifetime.
28|Read `include/fuse_lowlevel.h` semantics first.
29|
30|### 2. Start from official examples
31|
32|Check the `example/` directory in `libfuse/libfuse` before drafting handlers from scratch.
33|For passthrough, mirror, hello-world, or minimal callback wiring, adapt an official example instead of inventing a new skeleton.
34|
35|### 3. Build correctly
36|
37|Use these defaults unless the project already defines them:
38|
39|```bash
40|pkg-config fuse3 --cflags --libs
41|```
42|
43|Typical manual build pattern:
44|
45|```bash
46|gcc fs.c -o fs $(pkg-config fuse3 --cflags --libs)
47|```
48|
49|If the project vendors `libfuse`, follow its existing Meson/Ninja setup instead of replacing the build flow.
50|
51|### 4. Run and debug safely
52|
53|Use a writable, non-sticky mountpoint owned by the current user.
54|Start in foreground debug mode first:
55|
56|```bash
57|./fs -f -d <mountpoint>
58|```
59|
60|If mounting fails, check:
61|- `fusermount3` availability
62|- `/etc/fuse.conf`
63|- `allow_other` vs `default_permissions`
64|- whether the mountpoint is writable by the mounting user
65|
66|### 5. Troubleshoot by symptom
67|
68|If callbacks are not firing, verify the mount succeeded and the process is still in foreground.
69|If permission behavior is surprising, inspect `default_permissions` and `allow_other`.
70|If the filesystem hangs, inspect whether a low-level handler failed to send a reply.
71|If performance is poor, check whether the design needs low-level API control, cache tuning, or fewer round trips.
72|
73|## Read Next
74|

2|name: btrfs
3|description: >
4|  Btrfs filesystem administration: subvolumes, snapshots, rollback, balance,
5|  scrub, RAID profiles, compression, quotas, send/receive backups, and
6|  troubleshooting.
7|  MUST consult when installing, configuring, or troubleshooting btrfs.
8|triggerPhrases:
9|  - "btrfs"
10|  - "Btrfs"
11|  - "btrfs snapshot"
12|  - "btrfs subvolume"
13|  - "btrfs balance"
14|  - "btrfs scrub"
15|  - "copy-on-write filesystem"
16|  - "CoW filesystem"
17|  - "btrfs-progs"
18|  - "mkfs.btrfs"
19|  - "snapper"
20|  - "btrbk"
21|globs:
22|  - "**/fstab"
23|  - "**/etc/fstab"
24|last_verified: "unverified"
25|---
26|
27|## Identity
28|
29|| Property | Value |
30||----------|-------|
31|| **Type** | Kernel built-in filesystem (no loadable module needed on most distros) |
32|| **CLI tool** | `btrfs` (subcommands: `filesystem`, `subvolume`, `balance`, `scrub`, `device`, `quota`, `qgroup`, `check`, `defragment`, `rescue`) |
33|| **Distro install** | `apt install btrfs-progs` / `dnf install btrfs-progs` |
34|| **Create** | `mkfs.btrfs` |
35|| **Kernel version matters** | Significant stability improvements landed between 4.x and 6.x; older kernels have known bugs with RAID-5/6 and balance |
36|
37|## Quick Start
38|
39|```bash
40|sudo apt install btrfs-progs
41|sudo mkfs.btrfs -L mydata /dev/sdX1
42|sudo mount /dev/sdX1 /mnt/mydata
43|btrfs filesystem show /mnt/mydata
44|btrfs device stats /mnt/mydata
45|```
46|
47|## Key Operations
48|
49|| Task | Command |
50||------|---------|
51|| Show filesystems | `btrfs filesystem show` |
52|| Filesystem usage (detailed) | `btrfs filesystem usage /mount` |
53|| List subvolumes | `btrfs subvolume list /mount` |
54|| Create subvolume | `btrfs subvolume create /mount/name` |
55|| Delete subvolume | `btrfs subvolume delete /mount/name` |
56|| Create read-write snapshot | `btrfs subvolume snapshot /mount/src /mount/dst` |
57|| Create read-only snapshot | `btrfs subvolume snapshot -r /mount/src /mount/dst` |
58|| Rollback: delete current, rename snapshot | `btrfs subvolume delete /mount/@; mv /mount/@snapshot /mount/@` |
59|| Rollback: recreate subvolume from snapshot | `btrfs subvolume snapshot /mount/@snapshot /mount/@` |
60|| Balance start (all chunks) | `btrfs balance start /mount` |
61|| Balance start (metadata only) | `btrfs balance start -mconvert=raid1 /mount` |
62|| Balance status | `btrfs balance status /mount` |
63|| Balance cancel | `btrfs balance cancel /mount` |
64|| Scrub start | `btrfs scrub start /mount` |
65|| Scrub status | `btrfs scrub status /mount` |
66|| Scrub cancel | `btrfs scrub cancel /mount` |
67|| Check filesystem (read-only) | `btrfs check /dev/sdX` (unmounted) |
68|| Defragment file or directory | `btrfs filesystem defragment -r /mount` |
69|| Resize (grow) | `btrfs filesystem resize max /mount` |
70|| Resize (shrink) | `btrfs filesystem resize -10G /mount` |
71|| Add device | `btrfs device add /dev/sdY /mount` |
72|| Remove device | `btrfs device remove /dev/sdY /mount` |
73|| Device read/write error stats | `btrfs device stats /mount` |
74|| Enable quotas | `btrfs quota enable /mount` |
75|| Show qgroup usage | `btrfs qgroup show -reF /mount` |
76|
77|## Expected State
78|
79|- `btrfs device stats /mount` → all counters are `0` (any non-zero value is a read/write error)
80|- `btrfs scrub status /mount` → `Status: finished` with `0 errors`
81|- `btrfs balance status /mount` → `No balance found on '/mount'` when idle
82|- `btrfs filesystem usage /mount` → Data and metadata ratios show reasonable allocation (metadata should not be >80% full)
83|
84|## Health Checks
85|
86|1. `btrfs device stats /mount` → all counters `0`; any non-zero value means hardware errors, act immediately
87|2. `btrfs filesystem usage /mount` → check both Data and Metadata sections; metadata ENOSPC is the most common silent failure
88|3. `btrfs scrub status /mount` → verify last scrub completed with no errors; schedule scrubs monthly via systemd timer or cron
89|4. `btrfs subvolume list /mount` → audit snapshot count; accumulation fills disk without appearing in normal `df` output
90|
91|## Common Failures
92|
93|| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
94||---------|-------|-----|
95|| `no space left on device` but `df` shows free space | Metadata chunks exhausted while data chunks exist | `btrfs filesystem usage /mount` — run `btrfs balance start -dusage=50 /mount` to rebalance underused chunks |
96|| RAID-1 on data but single on metadata | Dangerous default when adding a second disk; metadata is not redundant | `btrfs filesystem usage /mount` — check metadata profile; run `btrfs balance start -mconvert=raid1 /mount` |
97|| Filesystem mounts read-only | Encountered an error it cannot self-correct | Check `dmesg | grep -i btrfs`; run `btrfs check /dev/sdX` on unmounted device to assess damage |
98|| Balance fails with ENOSPC mid-run | Not enough free space to relocate all chunks | Use `-dusage=<N>` filter to relocate only partially-used chunks first; free up space before retrying |
99|| Qgroup show reports inflated usage | Qgroups track snapshot references — shared data counted in each | Shared data is expected; use `btrfs qgroup show -reF` to see exclusive vs shared bytes |
100|| Snapshot accumulation fills disk | Old snapshots reference deleted data, preventing space reclaim | `btrfs subvolume list /mount | grep snapshot` — delete old snapshots with `btrfs subvolume delete` |
101|| `btrfs check --repair` made it worse | `--repair` is not safe for general use and can corrupt data | Never run `--repair` without consulting upstream; use `rescue` subcommands instead |
102|| Filesystem errors after kernel upgrade | Older on-disk format or regression | Check `dmesg`; downgrade kernel or use `btrfs rescue` tools; check known issues for your kernel version |
103|
104|## Pain Points
105|
106|- **ENOSPC due to metadata/data imbalance**: The most common Btrfs "gotcha". Btrfs allocates space in chunks — if metadata chunks fill up, writes fail even when data chunks are available and `df` still shows free space. Fix: `btrfs balance start -dusage=50 /mount` to reclaim partially-empty chunks. This is not a bug — it is the expected behavior when chunk allocation becomes imbalanced.
107|- **Mixed RAID profiles between data and metadata**: Adding a second disk does not automatically mirror metadata. A system can have `RAID1` data but `single` metadata, meaning metadata loss on one disk is fatal. Always explicitly set both with `-d` and `-m` flags.
108|- **Snapshots are instant but they accumulate**: Snapshot creation is O(1) and free. Deletion requires reference counting and can be slow. Unreferenced snapshots hold on to deleted data indefinitely — disk usage only decreases after snapshot deletion completes.
109|- **`btrfs check` is slow and `--repair` is risky**: Unlike `fsck.ext4`, Btrfs check does not have a safe repair mode. `--repair` can corrupt a filesystem that `check` reports as damaged. Prefer `btrfs rescue` subcommands (`zero-log`, `fix-device-size`) for targeted fixes.
110|- **Btrfs RAID-5/6 has known parity issues**: As of kernels through 6.x, Btrfs RAID-5 and RAID-6 have unresolved write-hole bugs. Do not use RAID-5/6 for data you care about. Use RAID-1 or RAID-10 instead.
111|- **Send/receive for backups**: `btrfs send` / `btrfs receive` is efficient for incremental backups using read-only snapshots as base references. Tools like `snapper` and `btrbk` automate the snapshot lifecycle and send/receive workflow — prefer them over manual scripting.
112|- **CoW fragmentation on databases and VMs**: Copy-on-write writes new data to new locations, which fragments sequential files over time. Use `nodatacow` mount option (or `chattr +C`) for VM disk images, database files, and other large randomly-written files. `nodatacow` also disables checksums for those files.
113|
114|## See Also
115|
116|- **ext4** — Traditional Linux filesystem without CoW overhead; use when you need maximum compatibility and don't need snapshots
117|- **xfs** — High-performance filesystem for large sequential I/O; use for databases and media workloads where CoW fragmentation is a concern
118|- **zfs** — Full storage stack with pooling and replication; use when you need enterprise-grade checksums and send/receive without kernel version sensitivity
119|- **lvm** — Logical volume manager; provides snapshot and resize capabilities at the block layer beneath btrfs
120|
121|## References
122|
123|See `references/` for:
124|- `btrfs-options.md` — mkfs and mount options organized by category
125|- `common-patterns.md` — filesystem setup, subvolume layouts, snapshots, rollback, backup, RAID, and compression
126|- `docs.md` — official documentation and community links","total_lines":126,"file_size":8377,"truncated":false,"is_binary":false,"is_image":false,"not_found":false}

2|name: rust-memory-optimization
3|description: |
4|  Memory optimization and allocation reduction in Rust. Use when:
5|  - User is designing memory-sensitive or low-latency systems
6|  - Optimizing data structures to reduce memory footprint
7|  - Replacing heap allocations with stack-allocated/bounded structures (SmallVec, ArrayVec, ThinVec)
8|  - Handling small strings with optimizations (CompactString)
9|  - Reusing collections via clear() in loops
10|  - Implementing zero-copy decoding and references
11|  - Structuring arena-allocated memory (Bumpalo)
12|  - Measuring memory usage, profiling heap, or diagnosing leaks
13|---
14|
15|
16|
17|## Quick Navigation
18|
19|- [references/stack_allocations.md](references/stack_allocations.md)
20|- [references/arenas.md](references/arenas.md)
21|
22|# Rust Memory Optimization Guide
23|
24|Advanced strategies for reducing allocations, shrinking layout sizes, and boosting performance.
25|
26|## Core Rules & Patterns
27|
28|### 1. Bounded Heap-Free Collections
29|For collections that are usually small, avoid standard vectors to bypass heap allocations.
30|- **`SmallVec`**: Stack-allocated up to a threshold, overflows to the heap.
31|- **`ArrayVec`**: Fixed-capacity array wrapper; never allocates on the heap.
32|- **`ThinVec`**: Only takes a single pointer size when empty, reducing size in enum layouts.
33|
34|```rust
35|use smallvec::{smallvec, SmallVec};
36|use arrayvec::ArrayVec;
37|
38|// SmallVec: Allocates 4 items on the stack. Goes to heap only if count > 4.
39|let mut local_tags: SmallVec<[String; 4]> = smallvec![];
40|local_tags.push("Rust".to_string());
41|
42|// ArrayVec: Absolute limit of 8 items on the stack. No heap overflow.
43|let mut coordinates: ArrayVec<f64, 8> = ArrayVec::new();
44|coordinates.push(42.0);
45|```
46|
47|### 2. Small String Optimization (SSO)
48|Standard `String` consumes 24 bytes and allocates heap space immediately. Use `CompactString` for inline small strings (under 24 bytes) without allocating.
49|
50|```rust
51|use compact_str::CompactString;
52|
53|// No heap allocation for strings <= 24 characters
54|let username = CompactString::new("user_123");
55|```
56|
57|### 3. Boxed Slices vs Vectors
58|If a collection's size is determined once at initialization and never changes, convert it from `Vec<T>` to `Box<[T]>` to save 8 bytes of stack capacity space.
59|
60|```rust
61|let items_vec: Vec<i32> = vec![1, 2, 3];
62|
63|// Save capacity field (shrinks stack representation from 24 to 16 bytes)
64|let items_slice: Box<[i32]> = items_vec.into_boxed_slice();
65|```
66|
67|### 4. Zero-Copy Patterns
68|Instead of cloning or allocating strings, hold references to existing memory using slices or crates like `bytes::Bytes`.
69|
70|```rust
71|use bytes::Bytes;
72|
73|pub struct Message {
74|    // Zero-copy reference-counted byte buffer slice
75|    pub payload: Bytes,
76|}
77|
78|// Can be sliced and shared among threads without cloning underlying memory
79|let original = Bytes::from(vec![0; 1024]);
80|let slice = original.slice(0..100); 
81|```
82|
83|### 5. Arena Allocation
84|For batch allocation where structures share a lifecycle (e.g. AST parsing), use arena allocators (`bumpalo`) to allocate items sequentially in a continuous region of memory and free them all at once.
85|
86|```rust
87|use bumpalo::Bump;
88|
89|let bump = Bump::new();
90|
91|// Allocates quickly on the bump arena
92|let string_ref = bump.alloc_str("dynamic string");
93|let int_ref = bump.alloc(42);
94|
95|// Entire arena is cleared at once on drop
96|```
97|
98|### 6. Collection Reuse
99|Reuse collection allocations in performance-critical loops with `.clear()` instead of re-instantiating.
100|
101|```rust
102|// Bad: Allocates a new vector every iteration
103|for item in feed {
104|    let mut batch = Vec::new();
105|    batch.push(item);
106|}
107|
108|// Good: Reuses allocation buffer
109|let mut batch = Vec::with_capacity(100);
110|for item in feed {
111|    batch.clear();
112|    batch.push(item);
113|}
114|```
115|
116|## Layout Awareness
117|
118|Use `std::mem::size_of` to understand data layout.
119|
120|```rust
121|println!("User size: {}", std::mem::size_of::<User>());
122|```
123|
124|Reorder fields to reduce padding only when the type is numerous or hot.
125|
126|```rust
127|// Often smaller: group large-alignment fields first
128|struct Record {
129|    id: u64,
130|    flags: u32,
131|    kind: u8,
132|}
133|```
134|
135|## String Strategy
136|
137|```rust
138|fn label<'a>(name: &'a str, fallback: &'a str) -> std::borrow::Cow<'a, str> {
139|    if name.is_empty() { fallback.into() } else { name.into() }
140|}
141|```
142|
143|Avoid `format!` in tight loops. Reuse buffers with `clear()`.
144|
145|## Zero-Copy Parsing
146|
147|Return slices into the input when the input outlives parsed data.
148|
149|```rust
150|pub struct Header<'a> {
151|    pub name: &'a str,
152|    pub value: &'a str,
153|}
154|```
155|
156|Do not force zero-copy when it creates unmanageable lifetimes for little gain.
157|
158|## ThinVec for Enum Payloads
159|
160|When enums contain `Vec` variants, `ThinVec` reduces the enum size by storing only a pointer when empty:
161|
162|```rust
163|use thin_vec::ThinVec;
164|
165|// Regular Vec in an enum makes the enum 24+ bytes even when empty
166|enum Node {
167|    Leaf(i64),
168|    Children(Vec<Node>),     // 24 bytes for Vec
169|}
170|
171|// ThinVec only stores 8 bytes (a pointer) when empty
172|enum NodeOptimized {
173|    Leaf(i64),
174|    Children(ThinVec<Node>), // 8 bytes for ThinVec
175|}
176|```
177|
178|## Cow for Conditional Ownership
179|
180|```rust
181|use std::borrow::Cow;
182|
183|pub struct Error {
184|    message: Cow<'static, str>,
185|}
186|
187|impl Error {
188|    // No allocation for static messages
189|    pub fn new(msg: &'static str) -> Self {
190|        Self { message: Cow::Borrowed(msg) }
191|    }
192|
193|    // Allocates only when dynamic
194|    pub fn with_detail(msg: String) -> Self {
195|        Self { message: Cow::Owned(msg) }
196|    }
197|}
198|```
199|
200|## Arc vs Rc Trade-offs
201|
202|```rust
203|use std::rc::Rc;
204|use std::sync::Arc;
205|
206|// Single-threaded shared ownership — cheaper than Arc
207|let shared = Rc::new(large_data);
208|
209|// Multi-threaded shared ownership — required across threads
210|let shared = Arc::new(large_data);
211|```
212|
213|Prefer `Rc` when data never crosses thread boundaries. `Arc` adds atomic reference counting overhead.
214|
215|## HashMap Memory Optimization
216|
217|```rust
218|use hashbrown::HashMap;
219|
220|// hashbrown's HashMap uses less memory than std's and is faster
221|let mut map: HashMap<String, i32> = HashMap::with_capacity(128);
222|
223|// Reserve capacity upfront to avoid rehashing
224|map.reserve(expected_count);
225|
226|// Consider FxHashMap for non-adversarial keys
227|use rustc_hash::FxHashMap;
228|let mut fast_map: FxHashMap<String, i32> = FxHashMap::default();
229|```
230|
231|## Stack vs Heap Decision Matrix
232|
233|| Type | Stack Size | Heap Alloc | Use When |
234||------|-----------|------------|----------|
235|| `String` | 24 bytes | Yes | Owns mutable text |
236|| `&str` | 16 bytes | No | Borrowed text, lifetime bound |
237|| `CompactString` | 24 bytes | No (≤24 chars) | Short strings that own data |
238|| `Cow<str>` | 32 bytes | Conditionally | Mostly static, rarely dynamic |
239|| `Box<str>` | 16 bytes | Yes | Owned fixed string |
240|| `Vec<T>` | 24 bytes | Yes | Growable collection |
241|| `SmallVec<[T; N]>` | ~24+ bytes | Only if >N | Usually small, occasionally large |
242|| `Box<[T]>` | 16 bytes | Yes | Fixed-size after construction |
243|| `ThinVec<T>` | 8 bytes | Only if non-empty | Empty or small in enums |
244|
245|## Measuring Memory
246|
247|```rust
248|use std::alloc::{GlobalAlloc, System, Layout};
249|
250|struct TrackingAllocator;
251|
252|unsafe impl GlobalAlloc for TrackingAllocator {
253|    unsafe fn alloc(&self, layout: Layout) -> *mut u8 {
254|        System.alloc(layout)
255|    }
256|
257|    unsafe fn dealloc(&self, ptr: *mut u8, layout: Layout) {
258|        System.dealloc(ptr, layout)
259|    }
260|}
261|
262|// For detailed profiling, use dhat, heaptrack, or valgrind
263|```
264|
265|Use `dhat` crate for heap profiling in tests:
266|
267|```rust
268|#[cfg(test)]
269|mod tests {
270|    #[test]
271|    fn memory_test() {
272|        let _profiler = dhat::Profiler::new_heap();
273|        // code under test
274|        // dhat prints allocation stats on drop
275|    }
276|}
277|```
278|
279|## Optimization Workflow
280|
281|1. Measure allocations and CPU first.
282|2. Identify the hot path and expected data sizes.
283|3. Pick the narrowest memory change.
284|4. Benchmark before/after.
285|5. Keep readability unless the win is meaningful.
286|
287|## Allocation Decision Rules
288|
289|- `Vec<T>`: general purpose growable collection.
290|- `SmallVec<[T; N]>`: usually-small collection with occasional heap spill.
291|- `ArrayVec<T, N>`: hard maximum size, no heap allocation.
292|- `Box<[T]>`: fixed-size heap slice after construction.
293|- `Bytes`: shared immutable byte buffers.
294|- `Bump`: many same-lifetime allocations.
295|- `Cow<'a, T>`: borrow unless mutation/ownership is required.
296|
297|## Anti-Patterns
298|
299|```rust
300|// Bad: cloning a large Vec just to avoid lifetime complexity
301|let data = original.clone(); // expensive and unnecessary
302|
303|// Good: use Arc or Cow for shared ownership
304|let data: Arc<[u8]> = original.into();
305|```
306|
307|```rust
308|// Bad: allocating inside a hot loop
309|for item in items {
310|    let s = format!("processing {}", item); // allocates every iteration
311|}
312|
313|// Good: reuse a buffer
314|let mut buf = String::with_capacity(128);
315|for item in items {
316|    buf.clear();
317|    write!(buf, "processing {}", item).unwrap();
318|}
319|```
320|
321|- Replacing every `Vec` with `SmallVec` without measuring.
322|- Keeping arena references after reset.
323|- Cloning strings to satisfy ownership instead of shortening borrow scopes.
324|- Using `Arc` as a default clone workaround.
325|- Optimizing layout for types created a handful of times.
326|- Using `Box<dyn Trait>` when generics would eliminate the allocation entirely.
327|
328|## Review Prompt
329|

5|
6|# Memory Safety Patterns
7|
8|Cross-language patterns for memory-safe programming including RAII, ownership, smart pointers, and resource management.
9|
10|## When to Use This Skill
11|
12|- Writing memory-safe systems code
13|- Managing resources (files, sockets, memory)
14|- Preventing use-after-free and leaks
15|- Implementing RAII patterns
16|- Choosing between languages for safety
17|- Debugging memory issues
18|
19|## Core Concepts
20|
21|### 1. Memory Bug Categories
22|
23|| Bug Type             | Description                      | Prevention        |
24|| -------------------- | -------------------------------- | ----------------- |
25|| **Use-after-free**   | Access freed memory              | Ownership, RAII   |
26|| **Double-free**      | Free same memory twice           | Smart pointers    |
27|| **Memory leak**      | Never free memory                | RAII, GC          |
28|| **Buffer overflow**  | Write past buffer end            | Bounds checking   |
29|| **Dangling pointer** | Pointer to freed memory          | Lifetime tracking |
30|| **Data race**        | Concurrent unsynchronized access | Ownership, Sync   |
31|
32|### 2. Safety Spectrum
33|
34|```
35|Manual (C) → Smart Pointers (C++) → Ownership (Rust) → GC (Go, Java)
36|Less safe                                              More safe
37|More control                                           Less control
38|```
39|
40|## Detailed patterns and worked examples
41|
42|Detailed pattern documentation lives in `references/details.md`. Read that file when the navigation tier above is insufficient.
43|
44|## Best Practices
45|
46|### Do's
47|
48|- **Prefer RAII** - Tie resource lifetime to scope
49|- **Use smart pointers** - Avoid raw pointers in C++
50|- **Understand ownership** - Know who owns what
51|- **Check bounds** - Use safe access methods
52|- **Use tools** - AddressSanitizer, Valgrind, Miri
53|
54|### Don'ts
55|
56|- **Don't use raw pointers** - Unless interfacing with C
57|- **Don't return local references** - Dangling pointer
58|- **Don't ignore compiler warnings** - They catch bugs
59|- **Don't use `unsafe` carelessly** - In Rust, minimize it
60|- **Don't assume thread safety** - Be explicit
61|
62|## Debugging Tools
63|
64|```bash
65|# AddressSanitizer (Clang/GCC)
66|clang++ -fsanitize=address -g source.cpp
67|
68|# Valgrind
69|valgrind --leak-check=full ./program
70|
71|# Rust Miri (undefined behavior detector)
72|cargo +nightly miri run
73|
74|# ThreadSanitizer
75|clang++ -fsanitize=thread -g source.cpp
76|```","total_lines":76,"file_size":2588,"truncated":false,"is_binary":false,"is_image":false,"not_found":false}

299|## Architecture — the load-bearing invariants (read these before touching plugins, state, or identity)
300|
301|- **Identity storage lifecycle (owner correction 2026-10-05).** Cozo owns identity-to-leaf/loop assignment and isolation. One immutable physical seed is shared through read-only views; each identity keeps its own writable leaf and the existing seven subvolumes. Only the external host provisioner may add a new blank leaf once, during explicit creation. Login, start, stop, logout, restart, bridge recovery and failed-start cleanup must NEVER add/remove Btrfs members. Start verifies/remounts the existing pair through the host mount owner; stop leaves membership and data intact. The bridge only verifies externally mounted storage and records logical attachment. Do not interpret `attached=false` as device removal. No root copies, snapshots, new subvolumes or OverlayFS fallback during identity provisioning. Never modify a seed while retained leaves depend on it. Older add-on-start/remove-on-stop guidance in source, handoffs and signals is superseded; do not restore it. Host release snapshot/send/receive below is a separate deployment mechanism.
302|- **D-Bus is the only control plane.** Every plugin is a D-Bus object at `/org/opdbus/v1/plugins/<name>` under `org.opdbus.v1`. No `Command::new(...)` subprocesses, no direct file reads for live state, no polling loops in plugin/service code. New backend capabilities register as plugins in `crates/op-plugins/src/default_registry.rs` — never as new gRPC proto service packages.

2|# build-golden.sh — prepare the golden btrfs subvolume from one release build.
3|#
4|# Populate the `golden` btrfs subvolume with the complete deployable content.
5|# Taking a read-only snapshot, transferring it with `btrfs send/receive`, and
6|# activating the received filesystem belong to the deployment process. This
7|# preparation script performs none of those deployment steps and never writes
8|# into the running host's installation or restarts a service.
9|#
10|# Layout created under $OPDBUS_ROOT (default /opt/op-dbus):
11|#
12|#   golden/                      the deployable subvolume
13|#     bin/                       release binaries
14|#     libexec/3tched/             application-only helpers
15|#     usr/bin/threetched          pinned threetched dependency
16|#     usr/share/op-dbus/          immutable config, catalog and provenance
17|#     usr/local/share/op-dbus/dashboard/  pinned production UI assets at root
18|#     sv/<service>/run            enabled application runit definitions
19|#     opt/                       immutable broker and provider runtimes
20|# Host secrets, grants, network/bootstrap services and writable data are excluded.
21|#     MANIFEST                   commit, build time, sha256 per binary
22|#
23|# Usage:
24|#   build-golden.sh                 # prepare and validate golden (default)
25|#   build-golden.sh --golden-only   # compatibility alias for the default
26|#   build-golden.sh --dry-run
27|#
28|# Retired options `--live-only` and `--no-restart` fail explicitly. Requires
29|# root to populate the btrfs subvolume. Never builds: run
30|# `CXXFLAGS="-include cstdint" cargo build --workspace --release` first (the
31|# vendored RocksDB in cozorocks needs that flag on modern GCC).
32|# `OP_PERSISTED_CATALOG_SOURCE` may name an isolated prepared catalog; it
33|# defaults to `/var/lib/opdbus/plugin-blobs` and is never modified here.
34|# `OP_RELEASE_DIR` selects the same prepared optimized artifact directory as
35|# activate-golden.sh; it defaults to the workspace's target/release.
36|set -eu
37|
38|OPDBUS_ROOT=${OPDBUS_ROOT:-/opt/op-dbus}
39|OPDBUS_ROOT=$(realpath -e -- "$OPDBUS_ROOT")
40|GOLDEN_DIR="$OPDBUS_ROOT/golden"

151|    chown root:root "$temporary"
152|    chmod "$mode" "$temporary"

163|        find "$destination" -depth -mindepth 1 -print | while IFS= read -r entry; do
164|            relative=${entry#"$destination"/}

168|                else

170|                fi
171|            fi
172|        done

175|        [ "$entry" = "$source" ] || ensure_directory "$destination/${entry#"$source"/}"
176|    done

178|        mode=0644

{"content":"1|# Local release activation
2|
3|The current native release controller prepares golden, transfers a read-only
4|snapshot with `btrfs send/receive`, and rotates read-only overlays directly at
5|the inventory's owned host targets. It retains active and previous slots.
6|The older per-file/current-symlink procedures below are historical, not an
7|alternative activation path.
8|
9|## Paths and ownership
10|
11|| Path | Purpose |
12||---|---|
13|| `/opt/op-dbus/golden` | Writable preparation subvolume; never an execution target |
14|| `/opt/op-dbus/release-send/<release-id>` | Immutable source generation used by the native transfer |
15|| Native filesystem roots `@release-a` / `@release-b` | Controller-owned received slots; never populate or select manually |
16|| Inventory-declared host targets | Read-only overlays selected by the activation transaction |
17|| `/var/lib/opdbus-release` | Protected controller state, transaction recovery and first-activation preservation |
18|
19|Retention is configurable per storage owner; there is no global five-subvolume
20|cap. Budget free bytes for preparation, send/receive and a recovery reserve
21|before starting writes. Count paths under the release root explicitly: `btrfs
22|subvolume list -o` on an ordinary directory lists descendants of its
23|containing subvolume, including unrelated Incus storage. Existing unrelated
24|subvolumes are not permission to delete storage. Preserve the category,
25|timing, vector and state subvolumes owned by cache/Snowball. Retain the previous active
26|release for rollback; retire only explicitly identified obsolete releases.
27|
28|## Current entry point and base prerequisites
29|
30|Run `sudo ./activate-golden.sh` from the repository root, preserving the
31|explicit prepared-artifact selectors described below. It validates the
32|independent root-owned release kit, provisions/reconciles slots, prepares
33|golden, then invokes native release/activation. It does not compile or reseal.
34|Use `/usr/local/libexec/opdbus-release/op-release-launch status` for the
35|authoritative slot, journal, overlay and readiness receipt; `rollback` selects
36|the compatible previous release through the same controller.
37|
38|Independent base prerequisites must be ready before the application cutover:
39|
40|- `identity-roots` restores only existing identity-root inventory. An empty
41|  inventory succeeds without provisioning; any failed restoration fails the
42|  service. Login/start/stop never add or remove Btrfs members. Its readiness
43|  marker is emitted only after successful restoration.
44|- On the restored host, the native Open vSwitch package owns its daemons.
45|  The runit `ovsdb-server` service observes the validated native PID with
46|  procps `pidwait`; its bounded check queries the actual Unix socket for
47|  `Open_vSwitch`. It must not launch duplicate daemons, change topology, or
48|  run the old uplink/bootstrap chain. Inspect sockets with native metadata
49|  and protocol tools; a generic directory listing can omit them.
50|- Independent `op-warp-endpoint` restores only the existing declared local
51|  endpoint from `/etc/op-dbus/warp-ssh.json`; `endpoint.sh check` verifies
52|  ownership, address/peer, aliases and MTU. An UP persistent TUN with
53|  NO-CARRIER is not evidence of SSH, remote ingress or authenticated access.
54|  This service does not restore MASQUE, firewall or policy-routing state.
55|- Logger definitions require the existing system `svlog` account/group and
56|  appropriately owned log directories. Long-lived helper services use the
57|  available `sleep infinity`, not an assumed `pause` executable.
58|
59|Runtime TLS, protected capability/toolset policy, provider keys and the
60|production router's matching configuration/token state remain outside the
61|release. The runtime MCP audience and toolset JSON files must be root-owned
62|mode 0600; the bridge rejects group/world-readable policy before binding.
63|Restore missing inputs only from a verified authoritative backup,
64|without printing secret values, overwriting present state, substituting
65|template grants or minting replacement identities. A router token must match
66|the same production gateway's persisted token hash; an unrelated historical
67|configuration is not recovery proof.
68|
69|On this host, `op-storage` and `op-storage-kernel-guard` remain persistently
70|OFF until explicit owner reauthorization. Activation is not permission to
71|rearm them. Enable the independent early-boot release hook only after a
72|successful activation receipt; do not reboot as a deployment check. A
73|received inactive slot is not a deployed application or a mounted 3tchedFS.
74|
75|
76|## Prepare
77|
78|Build the native glibc workspace, prepare its pinned UI and threetched
79|artifacts, and explicitly seal/persist with the freshly built `opblob` and
80|the service's schema-shaping environment. Preserve the previous catalogs and
81|review additions/removals before a live reseal. `build-golden.sh` accepts
82|`OP_PERSISTED_CATALOG_SOURCE` for isolated release preparation.
83|
84|Reuse already-built native binaries by setting `OP_RELEASE_DIR` to the complete

465|## Coding retrieval deadlines
466|
467|Coding retrieval has one total budget covering embedding and collection
468|queries. Defaults are 5 seconds for completion, 10 seconds for search, and
469|30 seconds for deep retrieval. Operators may set
470|`COGNITIVE_MCP_RETRIEVAL_DEADLINE_MS`, or override a mode with
471|`COGNITIVE_MCP_COMPLETION_DEADLINE_MS`, `COGNITIVE_MCP_SEARCH_DEADLINE_MS`,
472|or `COGNITIVE_MCP_DEEP_DEADLINE_MS`. Values are bounded to 100–120,000 ms.
473|Search reports failure when its budget expires; context returns an explicit
474|`retrieval_error` with empty results. Failure of every requested collection
475|also reports an error. Partial results remain available when at least one
476|collection query succeeds.
